articles.title: A quantum highway just one atom high could transform superconductors
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that atomic steps just one atom high can guide quantum vortices through superconductors, making them move more than 1,000 times more easily in one direction than another. This remarkable control over quantum motion could lead to a new generation of ultra-efficient superconducting electronics.
articles.content:
Scientists in Japan have discovered that tiny steps just one atom high can act like microscopic railroad tracks, guiding the movement of quantum vortices inside an ultrathin superconductor. Under certain conditions, these vortices moved more than 1,000 times more easily along the steps than across them. Researchers also found that they could adjust this remarkable effect simply by changing the temperature or magnetic field.

The discovery was made by researchers at the Research Center for Materials Nanoarchitectonics (MANA), part of Japan's National Institute for Materials Science (NIMS). Their findings offer a promising new approach to controlling quantum behavior and could eventually help engineers develop superconducting electronics that use far less energy while processing information more efficiently.

Why Controlling Quantum Vortices Matters

Superconductors are unusual materials that can carry electricity without electrical resistance when cooled below a critical temperature. This property makes them attractive for developing extremely energy-efficient electronics and other advanced technologies.

However, superconductors also contain tiny quantum structures known as vortices. These form where magnetic fields penetrate the material, creating small regions surrounded by circulating electrical currents. When the vortices move, they can generate electrical resistance and affect the performance of the superconductor.

Being able to control where these vortices travel could therefore help scientists improve superconducting devices. Until now, directing their movement in extremely thin, two-dimensional superconductors has been particularly difficult.

To investigate this challenge, a team led by Takashi Uchihashi at MANA studied an ultrathin superconductor whose surface contained a series of regularly spaced atomic steps. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, a technique capable of imaging surfaces at the atomic level, the researchers confirmed that the steps ran parallel to one another and directly observed vortices positioned along them.

The findings were published in the journal Physical Review B.

Atomic Steps Act Like Rails for Quantum Motion

The experiments revealed an extraordinary difference in how easily the vortices could move depending on their direction.

Using four-terminal resistance measurements, which allow researchers to precisely measure electrical resistance, the team found that vortices traveled more than 1,000 times more easily along the atomic steps than across them when exposed to intermediate magnetic fields.

In effect, the steps acted like tiny rails, creating preferred pathways for quantum vortices to follow.

"Our study shows that atomic-scale steps can act as effective rails that guide superconducting vortices, and that this guiding effect can be tuned simply by changing the temperature or magnetic field," said Uchihashi.

The researchers also identified a particularly interesting behavior when the magnetic field ranged from approximately 0.10 to 0.20 T (tesla, a unit used to measure magnetic field strength). Within this range, vortices could flow freely along the steps without becoming trapped by imperfections in the material.

This behavior, known as one-dimensional pinning-free vortex flow, means the vortices can travel along a defined path without encountering the usual obstacles that restrict their movement.

At the lowest temperatures, the researchers observed another unusual effect. Vortex motion was governed by quantum tunneling, a phenomenon in which quantum objects can pass through energy barriers that would normally prevent their movement under classical physics.

A New Path Toward More Efficient Superconductors

The findings demonstrate that even a surface feature only one atom high can have a powerful influence on the movement of quantum vortices.

By using these atomic steps as natural guiding tracks, scientists may be able to control vortex motion with remarkable precision. The ability to adjust that motion through temperature and magnetic fields also provides an additional way to influence how superconductors behave.

Although practical applications will require further development, this atomic-scale approach could eventually help researchers manage both vortex movement and heat flow in future superconducting technologies, potentially enabling more efficient devices that consume less power.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about controlling quantum vortices in superconductors using atomic steps, which could lead to ultra-efficient superconducting electronics. This breakthrough has broad implications for energy-efficient technology and quantum device engineering, offering a tangible positive impact on future electronics and energy consumption.

articles.title: History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03338-yCryptographers’ inboxes are being flooded with requests to validate cipher solutions.
articles.content:
Enigma machines were used by the German armed forces to encrypt communications during the Second World War.Credit: Ullstein Bild via Getty

Carter Leffen couldn’t believe his eyes when the artificial-intelligence model GPT-6 Astra decoded a secret German army message that had been encrypted for 85 years. Leffen, who has no cryptography experience, asked the model to decipher the message, nudged it a few times to keep thinking and encouraged it to keep working when he went to bed. Sure enough, when he woke up in the morning, it had a solution.

Leffen is one of many non-experts who are now using large language models (LLMs) to break historical codes. Their efforts harness the LLMs’ ability to rapidly deploy decryption algorithms while also searching the Internet for extra historical documents or information that might help.

Cryptography specialists are thrilled at the surge in interest in codebreaking — but they are also being overwhelmed by a deluge of requests to validate AI solutions, which can often be incorrect. “There are so many false positives that are coming in from people who don’t really understand cryptanalysis,” says Elonka Dunin, a retired game developer in the Washington DC area who has written books on cryptography.

Cracked codes

In September, Leffen, a product development coach at financial data and media company Bloomberg in New York City, asked GPT-6 Astra to scour Crypto Cellar Research, a website listing historical, unsolved ciphers that is run by independent cryptographer Frode Weierud in Oslo. Leffen tasked the LLM with selecting and then decoding a message encrypted by Enigma, a machine used by the German armed forces during the Second World War to hide military communications from enemies. Enigma’s rotors and plugs rerouted electrical signals to encrypt the letters of the alphabet in up to 103 sextillion possible ways.

AI is helping to decode animals’ speech. Will it also let us talk with them?

GPT-6 Astra, developed by the firm OpenAI in San Francisco, California, chose a message sent on 10 July 1941, possibly because it was short — 82 characters — and was potentially related to another Enigma message sent on the same date that had been decoded in 2017. If that already-solved message contained some of the same words as the unsolved one, it could help to ease the decryption, providing what cryptographers call a crib. For instance, both messages might be addressed to “Obergruppenführer”, a high-level Nazi official.

GPT-6 Astra wrote code to simulate an Enigma machine and searched for the settings that would both reproduce the crib from the message solved in 2017 and render the unsolved message comprehensible. In ten hours, the LLM tested more than four billion settings. Leffen was “gobsmacked” by the solution it presented to him and sent it to Weierud for confirmation. It turned out that the message had been encrypted with Enigma settings different from those used on the already-deciphered message, even though they were sent on the same day — this is unusual and might explain why the code went unsolved for so long.

The imitation game

Days later, inspired by Leffen’s success, Carter Church, a staff engineer at cybersecurity company SentinelOne in Mountain View, California, decided to tackle an unsolved cipher sent by an Italian official to one of French emperor Napoleon’s generals in 1809. Church gave GPT-6 Astra a picture of the message, which had been listed on Cryptiana, a website compiled by Japanese patent engineer and hobby cryptographer Satoshi Tomokiyo.

GPT-6 Astra found a partial key among records on a French cryptography website, and tried an incremental approach to tackle the unsolved message. It used a common decoding strategy called simulated annealing, in which a deciphering key is tweaked iteratively according to whether the output is more comprehensible than that from the previous key. GPT-6 Astra hit on a successful key in about six hours, and Church sent the decoded message — which turned out to describe troop locations — to Tomokiyo, based in Tokyo, for verification.

Carter Church used GPT-6 Astra to decode this 1809 letter, intended for a general in the French emperor Napoleon’s army.Credit: Persée/French Ministry of National Education, Higher Education and Research

Church notes that this message could have been solved without AI, but the LLM’s ability to transcribe the symbols in the image, find the partial key and determine how to apply it greatly reduced the time and effort required.

articles.title: Scientists have just voted to abolish leap seconds
articles.summary: Since 1972, officials have added 27 leap seconds to the universal clock, but in a meeting this week in France they have decided to abandon the practice
articles.content:
Since 1972, officials have added 27 leap seconds to the universal clock, but in a meeting this week in France they have decided to abandon the practice

The Schiphol Clock, in Amsterdam’s airport Panther Media Global/Alamy

Leap seconds, previously used to keep the world’s clocks in sync with Earth’s rotation, are to be abolished. Instead, universal time will be allowed to drift up to an hour from astronomical time before it is corrected. Representatives from 69 countries voted for the change on 15 October at a meeting of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) in Versailles, France.

As the gap between clock time and astronomical time slowly grows, the effect will eventually be “like living on daylight saving time”, but permanently, says Emily Akkermans, curator of time at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London.

For most of history, our clocks have been set by the apparent position of the sun in the sky. But in 1967, after the development of super-accurate atomic clocks, physicists defined an international time standard called coordinated universal time (UTC), based instead on the speed of a particular vibration of the caesium-133 atom.

Advertisement

Natural fluctuations in Earth’s rate of rotation meant periodic corrections were needed to keep universal time in sync with the sky. As the rotation slowed, physicists added extra leap seconds. Twenty-seven have been added to UTC since they were introduced in 1972.

Now, that strategy is to be abandoned. This is partly because technological systems, from stock markets to telecommunications to GPS, have become much more reliant on precise timekeeping. That means introducing leap seconds is more complex, potentially risking the failure of mobile phone networks or electricity grids. Previous leap seconds have caused websites to crash and disrupted airlines’ booking systems, says Setnam Shemar at the National Physical Laboratory (NPL) in Teddington, UK.

“Time is now so much more important and integrated into these systems,” says Akkermans. “What once worked has become more problematic.”

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Editor’s Highlights Sign up to newsletter

What’s more, Earth’s rotation has recently begun to accelerate slightly, raising the daunting possibility of needing “a first-ever negative leap second”, said Noël Dimarcq, who heads the BIPM’s committee on time and frequency, in a statement. The practical consequences of such a jump backwards in time are hard to predict.

Physicists have been debating what to replace the leap second with for the past 30 years. At the BIPM meeting, they finally voted for a “leap hour”, which means that UTC will be allowed to diverge from astronomical time for up to an hour before being corrected. That should ensure an uninterrupted flow of time for “several centuries”, said Dimarcq. The change will take effect from 20 May 2027.

Shemar emphasises that the effects involved are very small: “It’ll be many hundreds or even thousands of years before a leap hour is needed.” He adds that physicists will still be accurately tracking Earth’s rotation to provide information for astronomy and celestial navigation.

The leap hour isn’t the only temporal innovation being planned, though. The BIPM meeting also asked for proposals on a new definition of the second – needed because optical clocks are now much more accurate than the caesium clock that time is currently based on – and called on international agencies to start considering how to define a universal time standard for the moon. Overall, the changes “will have a profound impact on future timekeeping both on Earth and other planets”, said Dimarcq.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant international decision to abolish leap seconds, which will improve the reliability and stability of global timekeeping systems critical for technology infrastructure like telecommunications, GPS, and financial markets. This change has broad societal impact by preventing disruptions caused by leap seconds and represents a meaningful advancement in timekeeping technology with detailed context and future implications.

articles.title: Will physics be the next field to be turned upside down by AI?
articles.summary: AI has taken huge strides in computer programming and mathematics – physics could be next
articles.content:
AI is better at physics than you might think johnason/iStockphoto/Getty Images

AI has grown so adept at solving mathematical puzzles that critics fear the flood of new proofs it creates will overwhelm academics and actually set the field back. Until now, AI has had limited impact on other areas of science, but there are signs that physics may be about to experience a similar upset.

John Sous at Yale University says AI models may have an unfairly bad reputation when it comes to physics because of the way they are tested. Cutting-edge models have previously scored as low as 30 per cent on six different tests designed specifically to assess AI’s ability on tough physics problems, but this doesn’t square with the successes Sous and his colleagues have seen when using them, he says.

Checking the problems in the benchmark revealed a litany of errors and ambiguous definitions. Once corrected, scores soared to as high as 94 per cent. The problem didn’t lay with AI, but in the tests not providing the necessary information.

“I think anything that’s well defined, even if it’s very hard, I suspect that AI will be very good at it – arguably better than the best experts,” says Sous. “This is backed up by our data.”

But while some parts of physics can be very well defined – physicist Vladimir Arnold once said that mathematics is the part of physics where experiments are cheap – many aren’t. And it is in the new, uncharted, fuzzy and cutting-edge parts of physics where AI may struggle.

Sous says that interesting physics comes when we find something confusing, some phenomenon we observe in nature, a material or the cosmos that we don’t understand. It is then a physicist’s job to create a model, an approximation or a simulation that captures and predicts that phenomenon.

“That’s a very artistic, a very creative process,” says Sous. “Can AI really take the next step and do the full job of a theoretical physicist? Do end-to-end research: define, create, explore, test? The picture is not clear yet.”

One reason mathematics has been at the tip of the spear of AI progress is formalisation. This technique turns a mathematical idea into computer code that can be methodically checked; the process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, it is considered correct beyond all reasonable doubt. It allows AI to process a problem and know when it has arrived at a correct solution.

While some advances have been made in using formalisation to test physics, it is early days in comparison to mathematics. And physics problems can often be messier and harder to pin down.

What is clear is that AI is already being used by physicists, not only to write computer code and do maths, but even to design and run experiments. Logan Wright, also at Yale University, is now teaching a course on using AI in physics research, and says that the syllabus is constantly changing to catch up with developments.

The key, says Wright, is to create experiments where the inputs and outputs can be computer controlled. Then that control can be handed over to an AI that is able to pull the appropriate levers to explore the problem space and arrive at meaningful results.

“It doesn’t have hands, it doesn’t have eyes, it just interacts with the world through language and code,” says Wright. “So if we can set up an experiment in which all the observations are reduced to code, and all the actions are reduced to code… then AI can actually be very helpful.”

One such experiment currently underway in Wright’s laboratory involves analysing how different shapes of laser pulses affect a rubidium atom. The researchers use Anthropic’s AI Claude to control the laser pulses and gather data on their effects.

“Claude can now basically say ‘I think this laser pulse is gonna produce this output’, right,” says Wright. “And it can test that.”

Wright says that such experiments can run overnight and complete as much work as a human would in a week – and human physicists can even use an app on their phone to suggest ideas that come to them while they are away from the lab, and get the results when they return.

“It’s not going to be [the case that] all of the universe can be explored in that way. It’ll be like very constrained domains,” says Wright. “I think part of the next frontier of physics will be to make as much progress as we can in those domains.”

Wright says that it is already entirely possible that AI will soon design an experiment that humans don’t understand, ask humans to build it and generate exciting new results. “But just to be clear, just like in math, there’s a debate about does it count as science if we get a result that we don’t understand anything about,” says Wright.
